newsitem.title: USA: Clinton launches second term with unity appeal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton launches second term with unity appeal.

text.p: Bill Clinton began Act Two of a sometimes turbulent presidency on Monday, taking his oath as the last U.S. president of the 20th century and pledging to lead Americans toward "a land of New Promise" in the next one.

In an inaugural address on a cold crisp day, with the sun breaking through clouds on perfect cue, Democrat Clinton mixed the customary inspirational rhetoric with a pointed appeal to the Republican Congress to end their feuding and help forge a leaner, cleaner government for a new millennium.

"The American people returned to office a president of one party and a Congress of another," he said in a speech before thousands gathered atop Capitol Hill with a panoramic view across a red-white-and-blue bedecked Washington.

"Surely they did not do this to advance the politics of petty bickering and extreme partisanship they plainly deplore. No, they call on us instead to be repairers of the breach and to move on with America's mission ...
"Nothing big ever came from being small," he said.

Clinton, 50, buffeted by controversies and missteps early in his first term and looking like a one-term dud two years ago, took his second-term oath at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT) from Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist and turned to embrace his wife Hillary and teenaged daughter Chelsea.
Each got a presidential kiss on the forehead.
Despite personal controversies and policy headaches looming for him, Clinton started off not merely on a second term but on something of a second honeymoon with the public.

Several new opinion polls give him job approval ratings of about 60 percent -- the highest since he first took office in 1993 and high for any second-term president -- and express a general if modest mood of confidence in America's future.

Clinton, who doffed his overcoat and braved the cold hatless in a dark blue suit, also offered grand visionary words appropriate to the occasion and the special place he occupies "on the edge of a new century, in a new millennium ... on the edge of a bright new prospect in human affairs."

In a speech of about 25 minutes, he cited as a source of inspiration slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, who gave his famous "I have a dream speech" in 1963 from a spot Clinton could see on the horizon from where he stood.
Monday was also a national holiday marking King's birth. "Guided by the ancient vision of a promised land, let us set our sights upon a land of New Promise," he said.

Apparently offering the "New Promise" phrase as the signature slogan of his new administration -- as John Kennedy once offered "New Frontier," in the most famous example -- he said that promise would include things as grand as racial harmony to things as basic as a balanced federal budget and reforms of notoriously lax political financing laws.

"Martin Luther King's dream was the American Dream," Clinton said. "His quest is our quest: the ceaseless striving to live out our true creed. Our history has been built on such dreams and labours. And by our dreams and labours we will redeem the promise of America in the 21st century."

But his olive branch to the Republicans carried a special resonance in a town lately more accustomed to festooning itself in dirty political linen than in the bunting, flags and inaugural finery of this day.

Congress was only taking a day off from the wrenching procedure of punishing Republican House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich for ethics violations. It will complete that business on Tuesday with a House vote.
And the personal controversy spotlight will swing back to Clinton as soon as it leaves Gingrich.

A continuing investigation of the Whitewater Arkansas financial affair and a new one into Democratic presidential campaign fund-raising practices face him as well as an attempt by a former Arkansas state employee to sue him for alleged sexual harassment in 1991 when he was Arkansas governor.

Clinton -- who has been moving toward the political centre for some time -- backed up his conciliatory gesture toward the Republicans with more centrist messages including the balanced budget pledge on which he has all but outflanked them.
He went beyond that to preach of leaner government the way conservative Ronald Reagan once might have.

"We need a new government for a new century, humble enough not to try to solve all our problems for us, but strong enough to give us the tools to solve our problems. A government that is smaller lives within its means and does more with less."

He kept his foreign policy comments to generalities, saying, "We will stand mighty for peace and freedom and maintain a strong defence against terror and destruction. Our children will sleep free from tne threat of nuclear, chemical or biological weapons."
"America," he said, "stands alone as the world's indispensable nation."
The inaugural ceremony was to be followed by a two-hour parade along Pennsylvania Avenue featuring colourul contingents from all over the country, and by black-tie balls at night.
